slides.page_title: Why Shard At All: Scaling Limits & Cluster Anatomy

items: Bigger box caps out on RAM, IOPS, cost-per-GB
Sharding scales sideways over commodity nodes
Working set larger than one node's RAM
Write throughput past one primary's capacity
Dataset larger than a single server's disk

left.title: Replica set
items: Same data, 3 copies
HA + read scaling
Zero capacity relief

right.title: Sharded cluster
items: Different data per shard
Splits writes and disk
HA comes from the shards
Shard: a replica set holding one slice of data
Config servers: a replica set holding metadata
`mongos` is stateless, caches routing, forwards ops
Run many `mongos`, typically one per app server

blocks.title: What Config Servers Hold
items: `config.chunks`: key range to owning shard
`config.collections`: shard key per collection
Since 3.4 they must be a replica set (CSRS)
Legacy 3-mirror SCCC mode is gone
A sharded collection's data sits only on shards
Unsharded collections sit on the DB's primary shard

slides.page_title: Why Shard At All: Scaling Limits & Cluster Anatomy (cont.)

items: Disk curve climbing to full with no plateau
Single primary saturated on write ops
Index size past RAM: page-fault storms
Never shard early: ops cost, hops, irreversible key

blocks.title: Shard Before You Are Desperate
blocks.text: Draining chunks off a full node needs free disk and I/O headroom. At 95% full you have neither.

blocks.title: Pay The Hop
items: app, then mongos, then shard, then back
Budget one extra round trip in latency SLOs
One or more indexed fields, value picks the chunk
Chunk picks the shard: that is the whole chain
Compound keys route on the prefix, not the tail
Every document needs a value for every key field
Explicit nulls pass in some versions, never rely on it
Index on the key prefix must exist before sharding
Auto-created only when the collection is empty
No multikey (array), text, or geoHaystack key

blocks.title: Immutable, Then Not Quite
blocks.text: Since 4.2 you can update a shard key value, but only inside a transaction or a retryable write, and it may move the document to another shard.

blocks.title: Keep It Small
items: 512 bytes was the historic key size cap
Key bytes live in every chunk boundary
And in every index entry, on every shard

slides.page_title: The Shard Key: Definition, Rules & Constraints

items: Cardinality caps parallelism: 2 values never fill 3 shards
40% of orders on one customer builds a jumbo chunk
Timestamps and counters send every insert to one shard
5.0+ `reshardCollection` rewrites under a new key
4.4+ `refineCollectionShardKey` appends fields
Refine only adds suffixes, never removes or reorders
Original prefix still dictates routing afterwards

lines: // index for the new key must exist first

blocks.q: Can I keep a unique index on `email`?
a_bullets: Only if the unique index is prefixed by the shard key
Global uniqueness on any other field is impossible
Enforce the rest in application logic, not the engine

items: A chunk is a contiguous range `[min, max)` of key values
Lower bound inclusive, upper bound exclusive
First chunk spans `$minKey` to `$maxKey`, all on one shard
A chunk is metadata, not a file on disk

blocks.title: Splits Move Nothing
blocks.text: Splitting a chunk copies zero bytes. It writes new boundary metadata into `config.chunks`. Only migration moves data.

items: Default chunk size 128 MB, 64 MB before 6.0
Configurable per cluster or per collection
Auto-split fired when `mongos` saw a chunk exceed threshold
6.0+ dropped auto-split for data-size migration decisions
Unsplittable: every doc inside shares one key value
Marked jumbo, then skipped by the balancer forever
A permanent hotspot pinning unbounded data to one shard
The number one symptom of a low-cardinality key

lines: // splitFind splits the chunk holding a doc

items: Standard bulk-load move: pre-create ranges first
Distribute the empty chunks before writing any data
Loader then hits every shard from the first insert
`config.chunks` records min, max, shard, and `lastmod`
That version detects a stale routing table on `mongos`
100 chunks of 1 MB vs 10 of 128 MB: counts lie
6.0+ balances by data size, not chunk count

lines: // docs, data size, avg obj size per shard

left.title: Ranged
items: Natural sort order
Neighbours share a chunk
Range reads targeted

right.title: Hashed
items: Partitions on the hash
Neighbours scattered
Range reads broadcast
Kills the monotonic hotspot: ObjectIds hash uniformly
Sequential inserts land evenly on every shard
Price: a value range maps to non-contiguous hashes
Ranged keeps `createdAt` between two dates on few chunks
Locality on the ranged prefix, spread inside it
Lets you zone-pin by `region` and still fan out writes
The middle path when neither pure mode fits

blocks.title: Three To Remember
items: `2.0` and `2` hash the same value
A float losing precision hashes inconsistently
Never use floating-point fields as a shard key
Sort order on a hashed key is meaningless
Sorted range scans still merge results from every shard
Zones need ranged semantics on the zoned fields
You cannot zone-pin on a purely hashed key

blocks.title: Equality Is Free Either Way
blocks.text: An equality predicate on the full key resolves to one hash or one range, so both modes hit exactly one shard.

left.title: Targeted
items: Key or prefix present
mongos reads chunk map
Contacts owning shards only

right.title: Scatter-gather
items: Key absent from filter
Sent to every shard
mongos merges results
Broadcast latency is bounded by the slowest shard
Tail latency dominates as shard count grows
10 shards means 10x the work for a one-hop query
Equality on the full key resolves to one chunk
A range on a ranged key hits the overlapping chunks
Prefix rule decides everything for compound keys
`SINGLE_SHARD` stage: one shard answered the query
`SHARD_MERGE` stage: the router merged many shards
Stage name tells you the path without guessing
`updateOne`/`deleteOne` once needed the shard key or `_id`
7.0+ allows them without it by broadcasting
`updateMany`/`deleteMany` always broadcast without the key
Sorts without the key: shards sort, `mongos` merge-sorts

blocks.title: Aggregation Split
items: Pipeline splits into a shards part and a merging part
`$group`, `$sort`, `$lookup` often force one merger
Merge lands on one shard or on `mongos` memory
`$lookup` on a sharded foreign coll needs 5.1+

blocks.q: Which query should pick the key?
a_bullets: The one you run a million times a day, not the pretty one
The natural primary key is often the wrong choice
Design from the highest-QPS read path backwards

items: Background process living on the config server primary
6.0+ evens out data size per shard
Older versions counted chunks and tolerated real skew
Acts past a 3-chunk gap, or the 6.0 size threshold
Critical section blocks writes to that range only
Short but real: migrations show up as latency spikes
Range deletion afterwards is asynchronous
Copies linger on the donor until the deleter task runs
They inflate `count()` and show in direct shard reads
Always read through `mongos`, never a shard's `mongod`
`disableBalancing` stops one collection, not the cluster
`moveChunk` / `moveRange` migrate a range by hand
Use them to drain a shard or shift a stubborn hotspot

blocks.title: Turn It Off For Backups
items: Filesystem snapshots need a still chunk map
A running balancer makes that map inconsistent
Some maintenance ops disable it for you
Since 3.4 one shard joins several migrations at once
Parallelism is roughly `floor(numShards / 2)`
Disk I/O and network burn on donor and recipient
A skewed cluster spends hours catching up after `addShard`
Zones, formerly tags, bind key ranges to named shards
The mechanism behind locality and tiered storage
Label the shard first, then assign the range
Zone ranges must sit on a prefix of the shard key
Zones use ranged semantics even with compound hashed
Balancer enforces zones first, evens out inside them
A bad zone can starve one shard and drown another
Overlapping ranges rejected; gaps float unzoned

caption.text: Your shard key is the one decision MongoDB will not let you take back cheaply, and most teams pick it from the field that felt like the natural primary key. This handbook walks the full chain: cluster anatomy, how keys turn documents into chunks, ranged vs hashed, why a missing key turns every read into a scatter-gather, and what the balancer is actually doing while your p99 spikes. Ends with the decision framework and the repair commands you hope you never need.
